item.title: India-New Zealand free trade agreement discussions to commence Monday: Mint
item.description:
India-New Zealand free trade agreement discussions to commence Monday: Mint

New Delhi: A high-level delegation from New Zealand is set to arrive in India on Monday to commence negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between the two nations. This marks the resumption of talks that were first reported by Mint in June 2024 and formally launched on 16 March 2025 by New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon during his visit to India [1].

The primary focus of the discussions will be to secure greater market access for New Zealand's dairy products, fruit, and wool, among other goods. The strategic move aims to diversify trade partnerships and reduce dependence on traditional markets, as the US has imposed an additional 10% tariff on imports from India and New Zealand, effective 5 April [1].

India, on the other hand, is expected to seek better market access for its agricultural products, textiles, and information technology services. The negotiations also aim to facilitate the mobility of Indian professionals and the creation of supply chain facilities to facilitate trade [1].

The current trade volume between India and New Zealand stands at $873.4 million, with India's exports to New Zealand valued at $538.33 million and imports at $335.07 million for the year 2023-24. However, exports to New Zealand have shown a significant increase of 32.26% during the period April–January 2024-25, reaching $583.99 million [1].

The key challenge in these negotiations will be New Zealand's insistence on increased dairy access, a point India has consistently resisted to protect its farmers. Despite this, India has already signed FTAs with several countries, including Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), and is also negotiating FTAs with Oman and economic blocs like ASEAN and the European Union [1].

The discussions come at a time when India is actively pursuing FTAs with multiple trading partners, including the US, EU, and UK, to secure better access for its steel exports. Trade minister Piyush Goyal has mentioned that the government is working on at least 10-12 FTAs to promote India’s high-quality, cost-effective steel sector [2].

item.title: US judge rules Apple violated order to reform App Store
item.description:
US judge rules Apple violated order to reform App Store

A US judge has ruled that Apple violated an order to reform its App Store practices. The ruling comes as part of a long-standing legal battle over the company's app distribution methods and commission rates.

The judge's decision, based on a preliminary injunction issued in 2021, requires Apple to allow third-party app stores and developers to offer alternative payment methods outside of Apple's ecosystem. The court's ruling is a significant blow to Apple's tightly controlled app distribution model.

The ruling follows a series of legal challenges and investigations into Apple's App Store practices, including allegations of anti-competitive behavior. Critics argue that Apple's high commission rates and restrictions on alternative payment methods stifle competition and innovation.

The decision has implications for both Apple and the broader tech industry. Apple has been under scrutiny for its App Store practices, with regulators and lawmakers in several countries, including the US, Europe, and India, investigating its business model.

The ruling also comes as Apple's App Store ecosystem in India generated Rs 44,447 crore ($5.31 billion) in billings and sales in 2024 [2]. The study found that more than 94% of the commerce accrued solely to developers and businesses, without any commission paid to Apple. This highlights the economic significance of the App Store ecosystem for developers.

As Apple faces this ruling, it remains to be seen how the company will respond and adapt its business model. The decision could pave the way for more competition and innovation in the app market, potentially benefiting consumers and developers alike.

item.title: Greer: Have standing call with India's trade minister
item.description:
Greer: Have standing call with India's trade minister

In a significant step towards strengthening economic ties, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal met with Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide to discuss the implementation of the India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA). The meeting, held on March 10, 2024, aimed to bolster trade and investment between India and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) nations.

EFTA, comprising Switzerland, Iceland, Norway, and Liechtenstein, is committed to promoting USD 100 billion in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in India over the next 15 years, with the potential to create 1 million jobs. This commitment underscores the strategic importance of the TEPA for both parties, as it seeks to enhance bilateral economic cooperation [1].

The TEPA was signed in March 2024, following extensive negotiations. The agreement is designed to facilitate smoother trade flows, reduce tariffs, and encourage investments. Among EFTA countries, Switzerland is India's largest trading partner, followed by Norway, highlighting the potential for significant economic gains from the partnership [1].

The meeting with Norwegian Foreign Minister Eide comes amidst a flurry of international trade activities for India. Earlier, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal met with UK officials, including Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves and Secretary of State for Business and Trade Jonathan Reynolds, to deepen India-UK economic cooperation. Negotiations towards a trade deal between India and the United Kingdom have resumed, signaling a renewed focus on strengthening longstanding partnerships [1].

The latest developments in India's trade policies also coincide with the U.S. Trade Representative's (USTR) annual report, which placed Mexico on its priority watch list over intellectual property rights. This move underscores the importance of intellectual property protection in international trade negotiations [2].

In a separate but related development, India has issued a strict 'Leave India' notice to Pakistani nationals following the recent Pahalgam terror attack. Pakistani nationals with SAARC visas must leave by April 26, while those with medical visas have until April 29. Overstaying can result in imprisonment and fines, reflecting the government's stringent stance on national security [3].

These developments highlight India's proactive approach to enhancing its trade relationships while maintaining stringent security measures. The coming months are likely to see further progress in implementing the TEPA and other trade agreements, reflecting a broader strategy to bolster India's economic standing on the global stage.

item.title: U.S. Trade Representative Greer: Initial trade deals to be announced in weeks, not months
item.description:
U.S. Trade Representative Greer: Initial trade deals to be announced in weeks, not months

In a recent development, U.S. Trade Representative Katherine Tai has indicated that initial trade deals are expected to be announced within weeks rather than months, signaling a potential acceleration in the administration's trade negotiations. This statement comes amidst ongoing discussions with various trading partners over the reciprocal tariffs imposed by the Trump administration [1].

According to a report from POLITICO, White House officials have been actively engaging with around 18 key trading partners to discuss the terms of the tariffs, which were initially announced on April 2 but suspended until July 8. The administration has been receiving preliminary outlines from these countries, which serve as a foundation for further negotiations [2].

The U.S. Trade Representative's office has emphasized the importance of addressing intellectual property rights concerns, as highlighted in the annual Special 301 Report. Mexico, which had been on the watch list for several years, has been moved to a higher priority group due to longstanding issues related to trademark counterfeiting and protection of pharmaceutical-related intellectual property [3].

The acceleration in trade deal announcements is aimed at alleviating concerns about the U.S. economic outlook, which has been negatively impacted by existing tariffs on China, autos, steel, and aluminum. The White House has been touting progress in negotiations, despite private indications that the discussions are still in the preliminary stages [2].

The administration's strategy appears to be to use the preliminary outlines submitted by trading partners to set the parameters for negotiations, with a focus on reducing trade barriers and increasing reciprocal trade. However, the timeline for these negotiations remains uncertain, with some countries expressing skepticism about the feasibility of reaching agreements within the self-imposed July 8 deadline [2].

In conclusion, the U.S. Trade Representative's office is working to expedite trade deal announcements, with an emphasis on addressing intellectual property rights concerns and reducing trade barriers. The acceleration in negotiations aims to mitigate the economic impact of existing tariffs and demonstrate progress in the administration's trade agenda.

item.title: U.S. President Trump's first 100 days: Flurry of executive orders, federal layoffs, deportations
item.description:
U.S. President Trump's first 100 days: Flurry of executive orders, federal layoffs, deportations

In his first 100 days back in the White House, U.S. President Donald Trump has demonstrated a robust and aggressive approach to governance, marked by a flurry of executive orders, federal layoffs, and deportations. This period has been characterized by significant policy changes and a focus on reducing the federal workforce, increasing tariffs, and ramping up immigration enforcement.

Trump has signed an unprecedented number of executive orders, totaling 142, which is just 20 shy of the total number of executive orders signed by former President Joe Biden during his entire term. This rapid pace of executive action has been described as "almost one year of activity done in 100 days" by geopolitical strategist Taufiq Rahim [2]. These executive orders have spurred numerous legal challenges, as state officials, businesses, advocacy organizations, and educational institutions have contested various policies, including tariffs and immigration detention practices.

One of the most notable actions has been the implementation of tariffs, with Trump imposing significant import taxes on various goods. Notably, he placed a 145% tariff on China, prompting retaliatory measures and causing concerns about potential economic impacts. The Trump administration has maintained that these tariffs are necessary to raise revenue and cut taxes, but critics argue that they could trigger a recession and exacerbate inflationary pressures [1].

The Trump administration has also been aggressive in its approach to immigration, deporting 139,000 people who were in the United States without proper legal authority. This has resulted in a sharp drop in border crossings, with Border Patrol tracking 7,181 encounters in March, down from 137,473 the same month last year. However, the administration's actions have been criticized for lacking due process, as many migrants have been deported without a fair trial [1].

Moreover, the Trump administration has initiated significant federal layoffs, with approximately 280,000 federal jobs lost through firings and buyout offers. This includes layoffs at the IRS, which could potentially hinder tax collection and reduce the budget deficit. The administration has also floated the possibility of an additional 145,000 job cuts, which could further impact the economy and public services [1].

In summary, President Trump's first 100 days have been marked by a flurry of executive orders, federal layoffs, and deportations, reflecting an aggressive approach to governance. While these actions have been met with both support and criticism, their long-term impacts remain to be seen.

item.title: US House votes to rescind approval for California heavy-duty truck rules
item.description:
US House votes to rescind approval for California heavy-duty truck rules

The US House of Representatives has voted to rescind the approval for California's stringent heavy-duty truck emissions regulations. This move follows a series of actions aimed at challenging the state's environmental mandates, which have sparked significant debate and industry pushback [1].

The vote comes as part of a broader effort by Congress to curtail California's authority over federal environmental standards. California's Air Resources Board (CARB) has been imposing strict emissions rules on commercial trucks, which have been criticized for being overly ambitious and potentially disruptive to the national market [1].

The House's decision to rescind the approval for California's heavy-duty truck rules is a significant step in the ongoing battle between the federal government and the state over environmental regulations. The move is seen as a response to concerns raised by automakers and other industry groups about the potential economic impacts of California's rules, including higher vehicle costs and limited consumer choices [1].

The vote also reflects growing concerns about California's regulatory overreach and its potential to affect national commerce. California's regulations have already spread to 11 other states, representing roughly 40% of the US auto market. However, some states, like Maryland, have recognized the impracticality of California's timeline and have delayed compliance [1].

The legal landscape surrounding this issue remains complex. The Government Accountability Office ruled in March that the EPA waiver issued under former President Joe Biden cannot be revoked under the Congressional Review Act, which requires only a simple Senate majority. This ruling creates uncertainty over whether Congress can truly roll back California's authority without more complex legislative action [1].

The House is also gearing up to tackle other elements of California's environmental regime, including blocking the state from imposing stricter pollution standards on commercial trucks and halting its low-nitrogen oxide emissions regulations for heavy-duty vehicles. These moves reflect growing concerns that California's progressive regulatory overreach is threatening national commerce and consumer choice [1].

The vote underscores the ongoing tension between federal and state authority over environmental regulations and the potential economic impacts of stringent emissions rules. As Congress debates, the larger question remains: Will America allow one state's left-wing environmental ideology to dictate terms for the entire country's auto industry?

[1] https://www.todayville.com/major-automakers-push-congress-to-block-californias-2035-ev-mandate/

Ukraine's Deputy PM: Ukraine and US sign mineral agreement

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine and the United States have signed a landmark mineral resources agreement, marking a significant step in their ongoing efforts to bolster economic ties and support Ukraine's reconstruction efforts. The signing ceremony took place in Washington, D.C., where Economy Minister Yulia Svyrydenko was present for the final coordination of the agreement's technical details. The Ukrainian Cabinet approved the agreement's text earlier in the day, setting the stage for its ratification in the Ukrainian parliament.

The agreement is expected to provide the United States with special access to Ukraine's mineral resources, in exchange for continued military and economic support. This support is seen as essential for Ukraine's efforts to rebuild its infrastructure and economy, which have been severely damaged by the ongoing conflict with Russia.

The signing of this agreement comes amidst ongoing discussions between Ukraine and the United States on the broader scope of their partnership. While the immediate focus is on mineral resources, the long-term implications of this agreement could include expanded trade, investment, and strategic cooperation.

item.title: Trump: Interest rates should decrease.
item.description:
Trump: Interest rates should decrease.

U.S. President Donald Trump has once again called for the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates, expressing his dissatisfaction with Chair Jerome Powell's current policies. Speaking at a rally in Warren, Michigan, Trump hinted at his past criticisms of the Fed Chair, stating that he knew more about interest rates than Powell and that the Fed was not doing a good job [1].

Trump's latest comments come amidst a backdrop of economic uncertainty, with the Federal Reserve signaling a slower pace of rate cuts for 2025 due to concerns over sticky inflation and economic uncertainty [1]. The central bank has cut interest rates by 1% through 2024, but any worsening in economic activity could push the Fed into cutting rates sooner and by a larger margin [1].

Powell, appointed by Trump during his first term, has so far largely ignored the President's calls for lower rates, stating that the central bank will keep rates steady in the near-term amid heightened economic uncertainty over Trump's tariffs [1]. Trump has repeatedly called on Powell to lower interest rates, warning that the Fed Chair risks a U.S. recession if he does not comply [1].

Trump's economic policies have been a source of uncertainty for investors and consumers alike. His tariff policies, which have seen the imposition of tariffs on Chinese goods, Mexico, and Canada, have led to retaliatory measures from some countries and have contributed to a drop in consumer sentiment [2]. The tariffs have also been cited as a potential cause of inflation, with some economists warning of a risk of stagflation if the Fed raises interest rates to combat tariff-induced inflation [1].

Despite the economic uncertainty, Trump has vowed to strike new trade agreements with many U.S. trade partners, predicting that the U.S. economy may suffer short-term pain but will ultimately flourish under a more favorable set of international rules [2]. However, the on-again, off-again approach to tariffs has undermined the policy objective, as businesses and investors lack the confidence necessary to make long-term investment and hiring decisions [2].

In conclusion, Trump's call for the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates reflects his ongoing dissatisfaction with the Fed's current policies. The economic uncertainty surrounding his tariff policies and the potential risk of stagflation have added to the complexity of the Fed's decision-making process. As the U.S. economy navigates these challenges, the Federal Reserve will need to carefully balance the need to stimulate economic growth with the risk of exacerbating inflation.

U.S. Treasury announces agreement to establish United States-Ukraine reconstruction investment fund

The U.S. Treasury Department has announced an agreement to establish a United States-Ukraine reconstruction investment fund. This initiative aims to support Ukraine's post-war recovery efforts and stabilize the region's economic landscape. The fund will be co-financed by the U.S. and Ukraine, with contributions from other international partners.

The announcement comes amidst ongoing discussions about a potential peace deal between Ukraine and Russia. The U.S. has been actively engaged in diplomatic efforts to facilitate a resolution to the conflict, including meetings between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump [1].

The reconstruction fund will focus on critical infrastructure, housing, and social services, with a particular emphasis on rebuilding areas most affected by the war. The World Bank has highlighted the significant role the private sector can play in Ukraine's reconstruction, estimating that nearly $50 billion in aid has been pledged to support the country's recovery [2].

The fund's establishment is a significant step towards stabilizing Ukraine's economy and ensuring a sustainable future for the region. It is expected to provide a much-needed boost to Ukraine's reconstruction efforts and help rebuild the country's infrastructure, which has been severely damaged by the conflict.

The U.S. Treasury's decision to establish this fund underscores the international community's commitment to supporting Ukraine's recovery and rebuilding efforts. As the conflict continues, the reconstruction fund will be a critical component of the broader international response to the crisis.

Meta CEO: Improvements to recommendation systems increased time spent by 7% on Facebook, 6% on Instagram, 35% on Threads over last 6 months

Meta Platforms' earnings report, set to be released after the close of trading on Wednesday, will be closely watched by investors and analysts. The social media giant has seen significant improvements in its recommendation systems over the past six months, leading to increased user engagement across its platforms. According to the company's CEO, these enhancements have resulted in a 7% increase in time spent on Facebook, a 6% increase on Instagram, and a remarkable 35% increase on Threads.

The upcoming earnings call is expected to delve into these advancements and their impact on user engagement and ad revenue. Meta's financials are typically straightforward, with 98% of revenue coming from advertising on its apps. Analysts will likely focus on new ad technology, user growth, ad prices, and ad views [1].

Wall Street anticipates continued double-digit growth from Meta. FactSet analysts project quarterly earnings per share of $5.23, up 11% from 2024, and revenue to rise to $41.3 billion, a 13% increase [1]. However, the start of ad sales on Threads may bring more growth than expected, marking a slowdown from the 22% growth seen in 2024 [1].

Additionally, analysts may question Meta about international ad spending, given the recent shifts in policy from the White House. The company's revenue from outside the U.S. accounted for almost two-thirds of its 2024 earnings [1]. Investors will also be interested in how the trade war and recent fines from the European Union have affected Meta's ad volume and pricing.

Meta's Europe segment, which includes more than just EU countries, represented 23% of its 2024 revenue and saw sales up 23% from 2023 [1]. The latest fine from the EU Digital Markets Act, totaling €200 million ($228 million), may pose additional challenges for the company [1].

In summary, while Meta's earnings report is expected to show continued growth, investors will be closely monitoring the impact of recent policy changes and user engagement improvements on the company's financial performance.

item.title: Trump on economy: Give us a little bit of time to get moving
item.description:
Trump on economy: Give us a little bit of time to get moving

As President Donald Trump approaches his 100th day in office, his administration has made significant strides in implementing economic policies promised during his campaign. While some promises have been enacted, others remain in progress, with varying levels of success and controversy.

Tariff Hikes - Enacted
One of Trump's central campaign promises was to impose tariffs on various U.S. trading partners. Since his inauguration, he has taken significant action on this front. Trump has implemented tariffs targeting countries like Canada, China, Mexico, and specific products such as aluminum and steel. However, some tariffs have exceeded the levels proposed during the campaign, with China facing tariffs as high as 145% and Canada and Mexico hit with 25% tariffs. These tariffs are currently paused as countries negotiate trade deals with the U.S. [1]

DOGE Committee - Enacted
Trump tasked Tesla CEO Elon Musk with heading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) to cut wasteful spending in the federal government. While DOGE has claimed $160 billion in savings, the goal of $1 trillion in cuts remains unachieved. Musk has taken a step back from government work, raising questions about the long-term effectiveness of these cuts. [1]

Tax Cuts - In Progress
Trump promised a range of tax cuts, including renewing the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA). While Congress has not yet passed legislation to renew the TCJA or add new tax cuts, lawmakers have indicated that it is a top priority. Negotiations over the bill's details are ongoing, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expecting legislation by July 4. [1]

Deportations - In Progress
Trump pledged to deport as many as 11 million undocumented immigrants. While early reports showed deportations remained at previous administration levels, the White House points to sharp declines in border crossings and self-deportations. [1]

Federal Land for New Housing - In Progress
Trump promised to open federal land for housing development to address limited housing supply. In March, the Interior Department and Department of Housing and Urban Development formed a task force to study how to open some federal land for housing purposes. Officials have not laid out a timeline for action. [1]

Increased Oil Production - In Progress
Trump promised to increase oil drilling to keep prices at the pump in check. His administration has taken steps to streamline the process of setting up new oil drilling wells on public lands. [1]

Auto Tariffs: A Temporary Relief
In a recent move, Trump announced a partial rollback of tariffs targeting the automotive sector. The decision provides automakers with a two-year grace period to adjust their supply chains and reduce dependence on foreign imports. This move aims to curb American reliance on imports and facilitate the repatriation of supply chains. The automotive industry has welcomed the announcement, with some manufacturers planning new investments in the U.S. [2]

Overtime and Social Security Tax Cuts - In Progress
Trump proposed eliminating the federal income tax on overtime hours, tips, and Social Security checks. While the U.S. House's budget resolution bill has been passed by both sides of Congress, an actual piece of legislation outlining spending and cuts is still needed. The budget resolution seeks $4.5 trillion in tax breaks and $2 trillion in spending cuts. [3]

In conclusion, while Trump has made progress on several campaign promises, many remain in progress or face challenges. The economic policies implemented so far have had varying impacts, and the effectiveness of ongoing initiatives remains to be seen.

item.description:
EU to present new trade proposals to US negotiators next week - Bloomberg News

The European Union (EU) is set to present new trade proposals to US negotiators next week, as reported by Bloomberg News. This move comes amidst ongoing discussions between the two economic powerhouses regarding various trade policies and regulations. The EU's new proposals are expected to address a range of issues, including the trade of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technology and semiconductor chips.

The EU's trade proposals are likely to be influenced by recent developments in the US, particularly the Biden administration's Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion. This framework, set to take effect on May 15, aims to limit access to the most powerful AI chips and certain model weights from companies like Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) to keep cutting-edge computing within the US and its close allies [1].

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has expressed his desire for the Trump administration to revise these regulations, arguing that the world has fundamentally changed since the previous diffusion rule was released. Huang believes that the new rule should recognize the current global landscape and allow businesses to better capitalize on future opportunities [1].

The EU's new trade proposals are expected to address these concerns and potentially offer a more balanced approach to AI chip exports. The negotiations between the EU and the US are crucial for maintaining a stable global trade environment, particularly in the rapidly evolving field of AI technology.

The current date and time are 05/01/2025.

item.title: Lindsey Graham pushes Russia crackdown bill with 500% tariff on Russian oil purchases; Trump's position unknown
item.description:
Lindsey Graham pushes Russia crackdown bill with 500% tariff on Russian oil purchases; Trump's position unknown

Republican Senator Lindsey Graham has gained significant bipartisan support for his bill, which aims to impose steep tariffs on countries that purchase Russian oil, gas, and uranium. The bill, introduced on April 1, seeks to penalize nations that continue to import energy products from Russia despite ongoing sanctions and the ongoing war in Ukraine.

Graham's legislation, which has garnered almost 60 cosponsors, proposes a 500% tariff on Russian oil, gas, and uranium imports. The bill is designed to exert economic pressure on Russia and its allies, aiming to force a change in their policies and potentially bring an end to the conflict in Ukraine [1].

The bill's momentum comes as President Trump has hinted at the possibility of additional sanctions against Russia. In a recent social media post, Trump criticized Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting that he may not be interested in ending the war and that different measures, including sanctions, may be necessary [1].

Despite Trump's public comments, his administration has been focused on negotiating a peace deal with Ukraine and improving relations with Russia. The administration has not yet followed through on previous threats of sanctions against Russia. Graham, a Trump supporter, has long advocated for military aid to Ukraine and sanctions against Russia, while also praising Trump's peacekeeping efforts [1].

Graham's bill has already secured enough votes to overcome a Senate filibuster, with at least 67 cosponsors predicted by the end of the week. This means the bill could potentially override a presidential veto, though Trump's position on the bill remains unknown [2].

item.title: Hassett: Wouldn't be surprised if GDP data is revised
item.description:
Hassett: Wouldn't be surprised if GDP data is revised

In light of recent developments, Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, has hinted that the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data for the first quarter of 2025 might be revised. The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that real GDP decreased at an annual rate of 0.3 percent in the first quarter, primarily due to an increase in imports and a decrease in government spending. However, Hassett's comments suggest that there might be more to the story.

The BEA's advance estimate for Q1 2025 GDP was released on May 1, 2025, and it indicated a 0.3 percent decrease from the previous quarter. This downturn was partly offset by increases in investment, consumer spending, and exports. However, the potential impact of the California wildfires, which disrupted consumer and business activities in January 2025, was not separately identified in the GDP estimates. The destruction of fixed assets, such as residential and nonresidential structures, does not directly affect GDP or personal income, but the BEA estimates disaster losses in NIPA table 5.1, "Saving and Investment."

The timing of the downward correction in XRP, a cryptocurrency, has also been unfortunate. Ripple Labs is scheduled to unlock 1 billion XRP on May 1, worth over $2.2 billion. While the added supply may briefly pressure XRP, the impact is expected to be short-lived as Ripple's standard practice involves relocking the majority of the tokens after some are allocated for operational and similar uses. This sudden jump in supply could exacerbate the existing downtrend in XRP.

The bond market's volatility has also been a factor. President Donald Trump acknowledged that he and his team were watching the bond market, but he insisted that the bond sell-off did not force him to pause some tariffs. The White House has been focused on the 10-year Treasury yield as it aims to lower borrowing costs.

Hassett's comments suggest that the initial GDP data might be revised, but the extent of the revision is uncertain. The BEA will release the second estimate for Q1 2025 GDP on May 29, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. EDT. This estimate will provide more detailed information about the economy's performance in the first quarter of 2025.

item.title: 12 EU member states request activation of national escape clause to boost defense spending, EU Commission says
item.description:
12 EU member states request activation of national escape clause to boost defense spending, EU Commission says

Twelve European Union member states have formally requested the activation of the national escape clause to increase defense spending, the European Commission has announced. This move comes amid growing concerns about the bloc's dependency on U.S. forces and a push to strengthen European defense capabilities.

Greece was the first to trigger the escape clause, exempting its defense spending from EU budget rules for next year. This action has since been followed by requests from other member states, including Germany, France, Italy, and Poland. The escape clause allows countries to increase defense spending by 1.5% of their annual GDP over four years, as part of the EU's broader ReArm Europe package worth €800 billion.

The initiative, proposed by the European Commission, aims to bolster the bloc's military spending by €650 billion. However, the response from member states has been lukewarm. Many governments had already finalized their annual budgets when the proposal was announced, and some countries, particularly those in the north, have expressed reluctance due to their strong financial health. Southern European countries, on the other hand, are more concerned about the potential reaction of the bond market.

Germany, in particular, has been proactive in requesting the activation of the escape clause. The country's acting Finance Minister, Jörg Kukies, has emphasized the need for a significant build-up of defense capabilities to address the changing global security environment. The German parliament recently passed a constitutional reform allowing for greater rearmament spending, with the incoming government planning a €1 trillion package for military and infrastructure investment.

The EU Commission has invited member states to submit their formal applications by April 30, with requests after this date still possible. However, the Commission has warned that the lack of enthusiasm for the scheme suggests that its forecast of €650 billion in increased defense spending may be too optimistic. Some analysts, such as Niels Redeker of the Jacques Delors Centre, have expressed concern that the frequent use of the escape clause could undermine confidence in the bloc's fiscal rules.

Despite these challenges, the EU Commission remains optimistic about the potential impact of the ReArm Europe plan. If member states increase their defense spending faster, the total amount could exceed the initial €650 billion target. Additionally, countries can receive an additional €150 billion in loans under the initiative.

The activation of the national escape clause represents a significant shift in EU defense policy. While it provides much-needed flexibility for member states, it also raises questions about the long-term sustainability of fiscal rules and the potential for reform avoidance.

Greece, on the other hand, has triggered this legal tool to ramp up its own defense investments, signaling a broader trend within the EU [1].

The move is part of a larger strategy to reduce Europe's dependence on U.S. forces and bolster its own defense capabilities. The EU is facing geopolitical challenges from Russia and China, which have underscored the need for a more robust defense posture. Additionally, the EU's efforts to attract top American scientists and researchers, often referred to as the "U.S. brain drain," are also aimed at strengthening its innovation ecosystem and enhancing its competitiveness in areas like artificial intelligence [2].

Prominent European universities and research institutions are actively courting American scholars and scientists, offering substantial funding and visa facilitation to lure top talent. This includes the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) in Belgium, which has opened 12 postdoctoral positions specifically for American scholars, and Aix-Marseille Université in France, which has launched a €15 million initiative called "Safe Place for Science" [2].

The activation of the national escape clause allows these member states to increase their defense spending without adhering to the EU's budget rules. This flexibility is crucial for countries like Germany and Greece, which are seeking to rapidly enhance their military capabilities. The EU's commitment to academic freedom and innovation is also seen as a strategic opportunity to attract and retain top talent, positioning Europe as a global sanctuary for science.

The request for the activation of the national escape clause is a significant step in the EU's effort to strengthen its defense and innovation capabilities. It reflects a broader trend within the bloc to become more self-reliant and competitive in a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.

item.title: Secretary of State Rubio: Urges Pakistan to work with India to de-escalate tensions, re-establish direct communications
item.description:
Secretary of State Rubio: Urges Pakistan to work with India to de-escalate tensions, re-establish direct communications

In a bid to prevent further escalation of tensions between India and Pakistan, Secretary of State Mark Rubio has urged both nations to work together to de-escalate the current conflict and re-establish direct communications. This call comes amidst a series of retaliatory measures that have seen both countries impose visa bans and suspend trade agreements following a deadly attack in Kashmir that killed 26 people, mostly Indian tourists [1].

Secretary Rubio emphasized the importance of maintaining open dialogue and avoiding further escalation, stating that the Secretary expects to speak with the foreign ministers of Pakistan and India as early as today or tomorrow [2]. He also encouraged other national leaders and foreign ministers to reach out to both countries on this issue, highlighting the need for a responsible solution.

Pakistan and India have been engaged in a series of retaliatory measures since the attack. Pakistan closed its airspace to all Indian-owned and operated airlines, while India suspended a water-sharing treaty and downgraded diplomatic ties with Pakistan. These actions have led to increased tensions and a potential threat to the Indus Waters Treaty, which has survived multiple conflicts and is a lifeline for both countries [1].

The US State Department representative also assured that Washington is closely monitoring the developments and maintains communication with the governments of India and Pakistan at multiple levels. The spokesperson emphasized that the world is watching this situation and urged all parties to work together for a responsible solution [2].

While the immediate impact of Pakistan’s airspace closure on Indian air cargo is expected to be limited, as most goods move by sea, the long-term effects and potential tit-for-tat retaliation could strain broader diplomatic relations and increase operational costs for global airlines [3]. The Indian government is currently assessing the impact of Pakistan’s decision on air cargo heading from India to regions such as the Gulf, Europe, and the United States.

In conclusion, Secretary Rubio’s call for collaboration and direct communication between India and Pakistan is a crucial step towards de-escalating the current conflict. The international community must continue to urge both nations to engage in meaningful dialogue and work towards a peaceful resolution.

The U.S. Department of Defense has approved a potential sale of Patriot air defense systems and related equipment to Kuwait, valued at approximately $425 million. The agreement includes the sale of one AN/MPQ-65 configuration 3+ increment 3 radar set, one AN/MSQ-132 engagement control station, and two M903 launching stations. Additionally, the sale includes a Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement launcher conversion kit, AN/TPX-57v1 identification friend or foe, and Defense Advanced GPS Receivers.

The proposed sale aims to enhance Kuwait's defensive capabilities, enabling it to effectively deter adversaries and support its participation in NATO operations. The sale is expected to be approved by the U.S. Congress, with RTX Corporation and Lockheed Martin serving as the principal contractors.

Five U.S. government representatives and five U.S. contractor representatives will travel to Kuwait for up to three years to assist with equipment fielding and training. This procurement is partially funded by Norway and Sweden, contributing a total of 1.4 billion Norwegian kronor ($124 million) and 300 million Swedish kronor ($27 million), respectively. The funds will help Kuwait reacquire Patriot-type projectiles, sensors, and other equipment.

The U.S. has a history of supporting Kuwait's defense needs, with the country having previously received Patriot systems in 2017 and 2020. The latest deal is a significant step in strengthening Kuwait's air defense capabilities, ensuring its readiness against potential threats.

item.description:
Fitch Ratings: We now forecast global GDP to grow by 1.9% in 2025

Fitch Ratings has released its latest global economic outlook, forecasting that global GDP will grow by 1.9% in 2025. This projection is based on a comprehensive analysis of global economic trends and policy developments.

The report highlights several key factors influencing the global economic outlook. Notably, the U.S. economy is expected to slow down, with GDP growth forecast to slow to 1.9% in 2025, down from 2.8% in 2024 [1]. This slowdown is attributed to President Trump's sweeping tariff policies, which have led businesses to rush stockpiling goods ahead of potential import duties. The Commerce Department reported that the nation's GDP shrank at a 0.3% annual rate in the first quarter of 2025, marking the worst quarterly performance since early 2022 [1].

Additionally, Australia faces significant fiscal pressures, with S&P Global Ratings warning that the country's AAA sovereign credit rating could be jeopardized if election campaign promises lead to increased structural deficits and escalating debt levels [2]. The major political parties have announced substantial spending commitments, including funds for new homes, tax cuts, and enhanced healthcare expenditures, which could widen the fiscal deficit to 2%-2.5% of GDP.

In contrast, the acquisition of North Queensland Export Terminal by Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited is deemed credit neutral by Fitch Ratings but is seen as a positive step for the company's long-term global expansion [3]. The deal is expected to increase the company's global earnings contribution from 4% to 10%, supporting its international growth strategy.

The global economic outlook is characterized by a mix of challenges and opportunities. While tariffs and fiscal pressures pose risks to economic growth, strategic acquisitions and robust fiscal management can help mitigate these risks and drive long-term growth.

item.description:
WTI crude futures June contract falls 3.66% to $58.21 per barrel, lowest since March 2021

West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures for the June contract plummeted by 3.66% to $58.21 per barrel on Wednesday, marking the lowest price since March 2021. The decline was driven by a combination of factors, including potential Iranian crude re-entry into the market and anticipated increases in OPEC+ production.

The price drop comes amid progress in US-Iran nuclear talks, which raises the possibility of Iranian crude returning to the market, adding further pressure on oil prices [1]. Additionally, expectations of OPEC+ increasing production for a second consecutive month are weighing on oil prices [1]. The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, OPEC+, have been considering a faster unwind of production cuts to expand market share [2].

Oil sentiment may also be dampened by signs of slowing demand from China. Reports suggest that some Chinese manufacturers are suspending production and seeking alternative markets due to US tariffs, leading to fewer orders and impacting employment. Although not widespread yet, these disruptions could ultimately hurt oil demand, as China remains the largest importer of oil [1].

Despite these developments, hopes of easing US-China trade tensions could provide some support to WTI prices. On Friday, China announced an exemption for certain US imports from its steep 125% tariffs, sparking optimism that the protracted trade dispute between the two largest economies might be nearing a resolution [1]. However, the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent did not support Trump's claim of ongoing China talks, while Beijing denied any discussions were taking place [1].

The recent decline in WTI prices has been accompanied by a significant drop in crude oil futures for both WTI and Brent crude. WTI crude oil prices have lost over 16% this month, while Brent crude has dropped closer to 17%, the largest monthly decline since November 2021 [2]. The S&P 500 has been in recovery mode in recent weeks, recovering some of its steep early April declines amid an optimistic tone from Trump officials on tariff reprieves and potential deals [2]. However, oil prices have not seen the same support from investors.

Freight rates for ESPO Blend crude shipped from the Russian port of Kozmino to China eased further in April to the lowest since mid-January on higher availability of tankers, complicating the process of finding a vessel [3]. The cost of transporting ESPO Blend to China jumped to $6 million-$7.5 million after U.S. sanctions were placed on vessels involved in Russian oil shipments on January 10, as many vessels working at Kozmino port were targeted [3].

Crude oil futures order flow analysis indicates early signs of a bullish reversal, with strong buyer interest emerging at current price levels after sustained earlier selling [4]. The price has reclaimed and held above a previously important resistance level, strengthening the bullish scenario. However, a sustained move above the upper boundary is essential to confirm a stronger bullish breakout [4].

item.description:
US crude oil futures CLc1 close at their lowest since March 2021, at $58.21 per barrel

Freight rates for ESPO Blend crude shipped from the Russian port of Kozmino to China have eased further in April, reaching their lowest levels since mid-January. According to three traders, the rates have declined to around $2 million-3 million for April-loading cargoes, compared to $4 million-5 million for February and March volumes. This reduction is attributed to higher availability of tankers, as more non-sanctioned vessels have joined the ESPO market [1].

The decrease in freight rates means Russian exporters will spend less on transportation and consequently earn more for their oil. However, the cost of transporting ESPO Blend to China jumped to $6 million-$7.5 million after U.S. sanctions were placed on vessels involved in Russian oil shipments on January 10. Traders anticipate that these levels might be achieved again this year if no additional restrictions on Russian oil transportation emerge [1].

In contrast, U.S. crude oil futures CLc1 closed at their lowest since March 2021, at $58.21 per barrel on Monday, May 1, 2025. This drop was influenced by easing tensions between the U.S. and Iran, which raised the possibility of more Iranian crude returning to the market. Additionally, demand concerns persist amid fears of a U.S. recession within a year and potential tariffs weakening global growth [2].

The ESPO Blend oil price fell below the $60 per barrel Western price cap level for the first time in early April, as the international Brent benchmark plummeted to its lowest levels in years. The price has since fluctuated but remains around the $60 per barrel cap, according to traders [1]. Higher oil prices and lower freight rates may bring the ESPO Blend price back above the cap, complicating the process of finding a vessel [1].

item.description:
Dow leads turnaround as U.S. stocks open lower and climb higher

U.S. stock markets experienced a mixed day on Wednesday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) leading a turnaround after opening lower. The DJIA initially fell by 0.2%, but it rebounded to close 0.4% higher, marking its best performance since January. This recovery was driven by a combination of positive earnings reports and economic data.

The day started with a mixed opening across major indices. The S&P 500 was up 0.1%, while the Nasdaq Composite was down 0.2%. The Dow's early decline was attributed to weaker-than-expected earnings reports from several companies, including technology giants Apple and Microsoft. However, the market quickly reversed course, driven by strong performance from the financial sector, particularly in the banking sector.

Barclays reported better-than-expected profits in the first quarter, with pre-tax profit up 11% year-on-year and revenues hitting £7.7 billion. The bank's CEO, C.S. Venkatakrishnan, noted that the bank is prepared for potential economic slowdowns and market volatility [1].

UBS, another major financial institution, also reported strong earnings. The Swiss giant beat expectations with a net profit of $1.692 billion in the first quarter, despite the challenges posed by U.S. tariffs [2].

The turnaround in the market was also driven by positive economic data. The preliminary reading on euro zone first-quarter economic performance showed growth of 0.2%, which was in line with economists' expectations [3]. This data suggested that the euro zone's economy is showing signs of recovery, which could boost investor confidence.

The autos sector also played a role in the market's recovery. Despite earnings weakness, the sector rose nearly 1% after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order softening some of his automotive tariffs. This move maintained a 25% vehicle import rate but reduced the overall level as a result of additional duties on products such as steel and aluminum [4].

However, not all sectors performed well. Volkswagen reported a 37% drop in first-quarter profit, citing the impact of U.S. tariffs on the global car industry [5]. Stellantis also suspended its full-year guidance due to uncertainties over Trump tariffs, further highlighting the challenges posed by trade policies [6].

The mixed performance of U.S. stocks on Wednesday reflects the ongoing uncertainty in the global economy. While positive earnings reports and economic data provided some support, the impact of U.S. trade policies and geopolitical tensions continue to weigh on investor sentiment. As the market continues to navigate these challenges, investors will be closely watching for further signs of recovery or additional headwinds.

EU's Kaja Kallas: Europe can maintain sanctions on Russia if Washington starts lifting its own

EU's Kaja Kallas, the President of the European Commission, has stated that Europe can continue to maintain its sanctions on Russia even if the United States begins to lift its own. This stance comes amidst ongoing diplomatic efforts to address the conflict in Ukraine and the broader geopolitical tensions between Russia and the West.

Kallas' comments reflect the EU's determination to maintain a united front in its response to Russia's actions. The EU has been a steadfast supporter of Ukraine and has implemented a series of economic sanctions aimed at pressuring Russia to end its military intervention. These sanctions have had a significant impact on the Russian economy, with the country facing challenges in areas such as trade and investment [1].

The EU's position is not without precedent. In the past, the EU has maintained its own sanctions even as the U.S. has begun to ease its restrictions. For instance, in 2019, the EU continued to impose sanctions on Iran despite the U.S. lifting some of its own restrictions [2]. This strategy has been driven by the EU's desire to maintain a cohesive policy towards countries that pose a threat to regional stability and human rights.

However, the EU's ability to maintain its sanctions in the face of U.S. pressure is not guaranteed. The U.S. is a key ally and economic partner for the EU, and any significant divergence in policy could strain their relationship. Moreover, the U.S. has been a vocal advocate for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict in Ukraine, and its willingness to engage in talks with Russia could potentially lead to a relaxation of sanctions.

In the meantime, the EU's continued commitment to maintaining its sanctions is likely to be seen as a sign of solidarity with Ukraine and a commitment to its principles of democracy and human rights. However, the long-term effectiveness of these sanctions will depend on the broader geopolitical context and the ability of the EU and its allies to maintain a united front.

item.title: Trump: Biden put the country at fiscal, financial risk
item.description:
Trump: Biden put the country at fiscal, financial risk

The Trump administration is considering sweeping changes to a Biden-era regulation that limits global access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, according to sources familiar with the discussions. The rule, known as the Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, was issued by the U.S. Department of Commerce in January, just before President Biden left office. It divides the world into three tiers to control which countries can access cutting-edge AI chips, such as Nvidia’s H100 [1].

Countries in Tier 1, including 17 US allies and Taiwan, face no restrictions. Tier 2 countries are subject to volume caps, while countries of concern—like China, Russia, and Iran—are banned entirely. The Trump administration is now discussing scrapping the tiered system in favor of a global licensing regime based on government-to-government agreements [1].

Such a move would align with President Trump’s broader strategy of negotiating bilateral trade deals and could strengthen the US’s position in trade talks by using chip access as leverage. Former Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross has indicated that some voices are pushing for the elimination of the tiers, although the administration is still in the process of finalizing these changes [1].

The administration is also weighing changes to licensing thresholds. Under current rules, orders below the equivalent of 1,700 Nvidia H100 chips require only notification. Trump’s team may lower that threshold to 500 chips, according to one source [1].

Critics, including Oracle and Nvidia, argue that the rule may push countries to buy from China, while some lawmakers warn it could backfire. Seven Republican senators have urged the Commerce Department to withdraw the rule, citing national security and competitiveness concerns [1].

The rule takes effect on May 15. A Commerce Department spokesperson declined to comment on the potential changes [1].

item.description:
Indian airspace shut for Pakistan aircraft from April 30 to May 23

India has taken a significant step in its ongoing tensions with Pakistan by closing its airspace to all Pakistani-registered, operated, or leased aircraft, including both commercial airlines and military flights. The move, effective from April 30 to May 23, 2025, is a direct response to Pakistan's earlier airspace closure in retaliation for the recent terror attack in Pahalgam [1].

The Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) issued by India on Wednesday, April 30, 2025, restricts Pakistani aircraft from entering Indian airspace. This includes both commercial flights and military operations, significantly impacting Pakistan's ability to conduct air traffic over India. The closure is part of a series of retaliatory measures taken by India in response to Pakistan's actions following the Pahalgam terror attack, which claimed the lives of 26 people [2].

The decision has immediate implications for Pakistani airlines, which will need to reroute their flights over alternate countries such as China or Sri Lanka to reach Southeast Asia. The Indian government has also hinted at considering a ban on Pakistani ships at Indian ports, further escalating the tensions between the two nations [1].

This move comes amidst broader geopolitical tensions, including Pakistan's decision to shut its airspace to Indian flights and suspend the Indus Waters Treaty, which has been a source of long-standing disagreement between the two countries. The closure of airspace is part of a broader set of measures that include the suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty and the downgrading of diplomatic relations [2].

The economic impact of these measures is likely to be minimal, given the small volume of trade between the two countries. According to the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO), bilateral trade between India and Pakistan is minuscule, accounting for just 0.06% of India's total trade [2].

The escalating tensions between India and Pakistan have broader implications for regional stability and security. The closure of airspace and other retaliatory measures underscore the need for diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the situation and find a peaceful resolution to the ongoing conflicts.

Trump: We're looking for rare earth all the time

The Trump administration has issued a series of executive orders aimed at accelerating the development of critical minerals from offshore resources. The orders, titled "Unleashing America’s Offshore Critical Minerals and Resources," highlight the strategic importance of seabed minerals to national security and economic prosperity [1].

The executive orders emphasize the need for immediate action to secure reliable supplies of critical minerals, which are essential for defense, infrastructure, and energy sectors. The United States controls vast seabed areas, holding significant resources such as nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese, titanium, and rare earth elements [1].

Key initiatives include:
- Streamlining permitting processes for seabed mineral exploration and development to ensure efficiency and competitiveness for American companies.
- Investing in deep sea science, mapping, and technology to support seabed mineral development.
- Establishing international partnerships to advance seabed mineral exploration and development technologies.
- Creating a robust domestic supply chain for critical minerals derived from seabed resources to support economic growth and military preparedness.
- Countering China’s growing influence over seabed mineral resources by strengthening partnerships with allies and industry.

Within 60 days, the Secretary of Commerce is required to expedite the process for reviewing and issuing seabed mineral exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits. Additionally, the Secretary of Defense and Secretary of Energy are tasked with assessing the feasibility of using the National Defense Stockpile for seabed mineral materials [1].

The orders also define seabed mineral resources and processing, and outline general provisions for implementation consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations [1].

This strategic initiative aims to position the United States as a global leader in seabed mineral development, ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical minerals.
